body: Great! I like this approach. Could you add documentation in the README?
Me too, thanks for doing this. How about moving it from "other_names" to "names.other", with "other" being an optional sub-field inside "names"?

@tauberer Definitely will do.

@konklone, I'd be amenable to that, but could it possibly be confusing to have a field named `other` parallel to things like `first`, `last`, etc given that it's `name` and not `names`? I may be paranoid, but I envision myself coming into a software project that borrowed this schema wholesale and being unsure of what that field is meant to store. Maybe `name.previous(ly)`? `name.alternates`?
Nah, you're right, let's just stick with other_names at the top level. :)
But at most one fec_id per term, right?

Sadly no; bachman raised money both for her presidential bid and her house race this cycle. The campaign finance limits are applied per race, I think, so the system probably reflects that; one can max out to her as a house candidate and as a presidential candidate.

Sounds like the simplest solution is just to make this an array - all FEC IDs which can apply to this person. I don't think the complexity cost of doing many-to-many between FEC IDs and individual terms is going to be worth it, but we also clearly don't want to just exclude any FEC IDs from the system because they're weird sometimes.

@jsfenfen, Oh er, sorry you said that the first time. :)

@konklone Sounds good. (An alternative would be to put the fec_id for _House/Senate races only_ on the term, where it seems to be at-most-one (and the placement would also code the election cycle), and either ignore presidential fec_ids or put them as you're saying in a list on the person-level id node.)

the FEC_ID for the seat they won.

We could do both? In the main "id" node, have an array of all FEC IDs, and then on each term, put all FEC IDs that were valid for them during that term. I actually wouldn't be bothered if a presidential FEC ID appeared on either their top-level or per-term lists.

Couple of thoughts - if we do an array of FEC ids, would we update historic legislator files to include new IDs if they happen to win election after a period of not being in Congress? I agree that some kind of look-up is useful, but I wonder if that's a separate file or whether we need to have FEC history in the "id" node.
Yeah, we would go back and update the historical legislator file with a new ID. My proposal clearly jettisons history, so if it's a vital thing to keep, we'd need to have a separate file.

So I think we've proposed 3 solutions - let's pick one:

1) Keep a separate file that maps FEC IDs to people per-term
2) Store a top-level array of all FEC IDs that ever applied, and store an array on each term of all FEC IDs applied during that term
3) Store a top-level array of all FEC IDs that ever applied

I do nothing with FEC IDs myself, so my preference is the simplest, #3 - since it seems like you could always answer the most common question (given this FEC ID, who does it refer to?) with that top level array. But you guys know the field better, so if you think #1 or #2 is worthwhile, we can do that, assuming you feel like doing the work to populate the extra fields and/or file.

I vote #3!

I think it's probably more correct to use the Constitution-set dates, because that person is still in power even when Congress is adjourned. Constituent services come to mind as a piece of legislative power that's orthogonal to adjournment.

Alright, I'll let you two decide how to handle the party switching issue. Though I should note: sometimes mid-term party switching changes party control in Congress, as it did in the 107th Congress when Jim Jeffords changed from Republican to Independent, so it could be important to note a little further than just an "oh yeah by the way" field.

But I'd like to continue to argue for the party abbreviation mapping. One thing I edited into my last comment (which was you probably didn't get via e-mail) was this:
"The other benefit being that we'd have the abbreviation for free if we want to, for example, have a party/state/district tag after the person's name."

So if someone wanted to display "Chuck Schumer [D-NY]", they'd have all that information for free, without having to reverse-engineer any of it. Similarly, if they wanted to display someone with a more obscure party abbreviation, like "Al Franken [DFL-MN]" or "Joe Lieberman [ID-CT]", they wouldn't have to do anything special—every party would be processed the same.

Along those same lines, the abbreviation/mapping would be a way to differentiate between party and identifier: DFL represents the "Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party", while ID represents "Independent Democrat", which is not actually a party. And "no party" is not strictly the same as "independent": George Washington is (almost?) always described as having no party, not as being an independent.

Wikipedia is an excellent source to get all this (IMO, important) information that the BioGuide might not make clear.

This is a very good point, I agree that people should have the ability to get those abbreviations (I didn't think that was the kind of abbreviation you meant). 

Not to be a stick in the mud about the separate file, but I think we can still achieve this without that, by having it be a second field. In other words, have both "party" and "party_abbreviation" fields. I only continue to push this because having to link files together is pain from a client parsing standpoint, and having separate files to interact with in our scripts is also a maintenance burden. I'd rather keep the data slightly denormalized.

Seniority resets, right? (if people leave and return)

In my experience, seniority is what leadership says it is. Some people, like Lautenberg, demanded that his seniority be restored as a condition of running again. So it _should_ reset, but doesn't always.

I was thinking about this some more, and I think that the benefits of having a separate field would outweigh the costs in the long-term (which doesn't necessarily have to start right this second).

There may be some usecases for having two separate fields and allowing them to vary independently, but I think for 99% of the cases, they would be redundant and would only add to the bulk of the filesize. (And they potentially run the risk of becoming out of sync by accident.)

On the other hand, having the parties be represented by abbreviations or codes means they can easily be used and referenced in multiple different places.

So here's what I'm thinking:
- Whatever party the person is currently a member of would be the code in the regular party field.
- If the person has previously been a member of another party, then they also get a list of other_parties that list party code and end date (and maybe start date, if deemed significant or necessary).
- The party file can then contain information about the party: full name ("Democratic Party"), short name ("Democratic"), what a member is called ("Democrat"), etc. Some of these fields can be optional—with some kind of fallback cascade defined—since an "Independent" or someone who is "Anti-Administration" wouldn't truly have a party name. The file could even contain website information or dates of existence, if desired.
- As Josh says, the most important party-related information for a particular term is which party the person caucuses with. So if a person changes from Republican to Independent, for example, but continues to caucus with the Republicans, then it isn't necessary to make any difference in notation of the terms. But if a person changes from Republican to Democratic, and thereby changes caucuses, I think it would be worth having an additional term to notate this. (Reverting my previous position of non-engagement.) Similarly, if a third party gains enough traction in the future, we might need a way to notate that a person is a member of the Green Party who caucuses with Democrats, or a member of the Conservative or Libertarian parties who caucuses with Republicans. (It might even be possible that different members of the same party caucus with different parties.) So the abbreviation code would be helpful here, as well.

So that's my thinking on what the way forward should be, but I'm not at all averse to letting things settle down before attempting to make any changes.

According to [Wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seniority_in_the_United_States_Senate), seniority is determined by the following factors (in order):
1. Length of continuous service
2. Former U.S. senator
3. Former U.S. representative
4. Former president
5. Former vice president
6. Former Cabinet member
7. Former state governor
8. Population of state based on the most recent census when the senator took office
9. Alphabetical by last name (in case two senators came from the same state on the same day and have identical credentials)

According to that article, Lautenberg has not actually received his previous seniority (because that wouldn't comply with these criteria) and is listed at 35th.
Good catch, I'm not sure how we missed these. Merged.

Because of this, if we were to list rankings, I'd much rather list them from an official source if possible. The House provides such a list [(PDF)](http://clerk.house.gov/member_info/seniority-112.pdf), but I think with the Senate it's limited to the "official algorithm" + "undocumented leadership fudging".

There's a tension between the terms list being precise and being understandable. I think there's (at least) 3 reasonable choices:
- Terms are broken up every time any one of the fields changes - the chamber, the party, the name of the person, maybe even some day their gender (I believe this has happened in other countries). Terms also are broken up by session and by service. The reason for a term ending is noted. This creates a lot of terms, and a lot of reasons. The parsing of this array to precisely answer questions is, for some questions, extremely complicated, and for others, extremely simple.
- Terms are broken up only by session/service, and show the state at which the person ended the term. (The way things are now.)
- Two arrays are provided, one that does the first thing (phases? roles?), and one that does the second (terms). This makes answering more questions easy, doesn't make any kinds of questions harder, but is a much bigger maintenance burden (and duplicates a substantial amount of data). It's possible the terms array in this situation could be slimmed down to be vastly simpler - just the start and end dates (and reason for ending).

No. 2 in that list is by far the easiest on we the maintainers. No. 1 is by far the hardest on client parsers. No. 3 is by far the hardest to _transition_ to for both maintainers and existing parsers, but the most precise and useful.

I think the terms for everyone serving from 1933 onward should be updated. (That's the middle of the 73rd Congress plus every full Congress starting with the 74th.) Per the 20th Amendment, all terms are from January 3rd to January 3rd except in member-specific situations.

It is arguable what the terms were prior to 1933, but I believe the BioGuide suggests March 4 to March 3. Wikipedia has had a debate or two as to whether that is indeed the case, or whether it should instead be March 4 to March 4. (I suppose the debate is whether the term ends at noon or at midnight.)

In all cases, I don't think it makes sense to list the Congress session times as the term delineations, because the people were members of Congress even when Congress was not in session. Before 1933, it was way more chaotic than that. Take a look at the first 86 years of the House and Senate:
http://memory.loc.gov/ammem/amlaw/lwsjlink.html

People in these sessions were elected the November before, sometimes started a session the March after, but sometimes not until _December_ - 13 months after their election date. I honestly am not certain whether or not they were sworn in on March with regularity, which could affect it, but I also don't know how we would tell.

I think all of us are in agreement on updating the term end dates from 1933 onwards, but I don't know that we've reached consensus on whether the start date should always be the 3rd, or whether it should be the day of swearing in. (I also don't know where we'd get the data to delineate the two.)

- I(3)(4): "The Vice President of the United States shall be President of the Senate, but shall have no Vote, unless they be equally divided."

Well, then can we agree on which ID is the canonical one, then? It seems kinda silly to continue to have a hundred different IDs for one person. Which one is the "unitedstates" ID?

My "crazy" comparison was a little congressional humor. But to your question, please read this Congressional Research Service report on the Speakership: http://www.fas.org/sgp/crs/misc/97-780.pdf. Among other things, it says:

"The right of the Speaker to vote has also evolved over time. The first rules of the House provided: 
In all cases of ballot by the House, the Speaker shall vote; in other cases he shall not vote, 
unless the House be equally divided, or unless his vote, if given to the minority, will make 
the division equal, and in case of such equal division, the question shall be lost.

The Speaker was thus prevented from voting on legislative matters, although the precedents of 
the House record several examples of Speakers voting contrary to this rule.

 The Speaker was allowed to vote in Committee of the Whole, but most early Speakers apparently refrained from 
this practice as well. At least twice (in 1833 and 1837) the House debated proposals to compel the 
Speaker to vote on all questions, but these proposals were defeated.

 It was not until 1850 that the rule was amended to allow the Speaker to vote at his discretion, and the modern form of the rule was not adopted until 1880. Rule I, clause 7 currently reads: 
   The Speaker is not required to vote in ordinary legislative proceedings, except when his vote would be decisive or when the House is engaged in voting by ballot."

and also:

"Although elected as an officer of the House, the Speaker continues to be a Member of the House 
as well. Accordingly, the Speaker continues to have the same rights, responsibilities, and 
privileges as all Members. However, because of the Speaker’s position as leader, it may be 
notable or even controversial when he or she exercises the powers granted to other Members, 
such as debating, voting, and sitting as a member of a standing committee of the House."

The same rights, responsibilities and privileges as all Members includes the right to vote.

Because the Speaker position was not clearly defined in the Constitution, the rules regarding it have evolved over time. But that does not mean that simply because it wasn't in the Constitution means that we can choose to ignore House rules and precedents. I would vigorously object to any attempt to impose our own view of what the Speaker can and can't do.

Derek's points all sound right to me. So far, there's never been a Speaker
who wasn't also an elected member, so - let's shelve how and whether to
record speakership as a separate field. At most, let's reserve ourselves
the right to add a boolean 'speaker' field later (which doesn't require any
changes to any of the field types we've talked about so far).

Yeah, my suggestion for how we might support Popolo and integrate more easily with others who use Popolo-compliant systems is that we have a transformer script that takes our current files and spits out Popolo versions. This wouldn't disturb any of our existing pipelines, allows us to continue optimizing our data's native representation for a US context, and isn't much upfront or ongoing work.

The Popolo output might or might not live in version control; if it did, we'd maybe want to wire that script's execution into our `utils.save_data` method. It might be easier for it not to, and we just have the script around for anyone who wants to use it. 

Either way, we'd want to write the Popolo transformer script in such a way that doesn't need to be updated unless we do something that affects fields covered in the Popolo schema. In other words, if we add fields outside of Popolo's purview, we shouldn't have to do any extra work because of it.

As for YAML in Popolo - we use YAML specifically because it makes for better diffs when the data is version controlled, and easier hand edits when the data requires some manual upkeep. For all other coding/integration/technical purposes, JSON is completely superior to YAML. I wouldn't make a Popolo YAML spec unless you want Popolo specifically to handle our kind of use case.

If we go with a script, it shouldn't be difficult to convert from YAML to JSON. The main work will be renaming fields and moving fields like `first` (for first name) up to the top-level as `given_name`. If congress-legislators defines additional fields, those can be kept as-is (unless they clash with Popolo field names).

I think the main challenge will be figuring out what to do with `terms`; there are a number of options.

I should note that I'm open to making changes to Popolo at this point, as I'm still collecting feedback to make it useful to a wider variety of use cases. For instance, Popolo defines no `identifiers` property for people, but it does for organizations; that's something that can be added to Popolo.

Popolo distributes JSON schema files at https://github.com/opennorth/popolo-standard/tree/gh-pages/schemas

We have two main criteria - it must be their "official" legislative account (not run by their campaign, but by taxpayer-funded congressional staff), and it must be verifiable. My standards for verifiable have meant either:
- Their official House or Senate account links to it, the Twitter account either links to their official site or no site (not their campaign site), and the tweets simply look non-campaign related. - We call their office and have a staff member verify that the account is run by their office's staff.

99% of the time, the first way is sufficient, and so we have a social_media.py script that automates the generation of "leads" by scraping through official House and Senate sites for twitter.com URLs (with a blacklist to handle weird embeds and known shared accounts). There may have been a difference at one point (probably as a legacy holdout from YouTube's pre-Google days), but that difference isn't terribly apparent to end-users or API users any more.  As far as I can tell, in 2013, the distinction between users and channels is blurry and meaningless -- a channel simply represents a list of videos that were uploaded by a specific user (ie. their public-facing profile on YouTube).

All(?) accounts have both a [userId](https://developers.google.com/youtube/2.0/reference#youtube_data_api_tag_yt:userId) and [channelId](https://developers.google.com/youtube/2.0/reference#youtube_data_api_tag_yt:channelId).  Most of those also have a [username](https://developers.google.com/youtube/2.0/reference#youtube_data_api_tag_yt:username).  Accounts that were created through a Google+ profile do not have a username, and have an automatically-generated userId that doesn't actually seem to be used anywhere.

[According to Google](http://apiblog.youtube.com/2012/03/youtube-google-api-and-you.html):

> Note that for accounts that have connected a Google+ profile to a new YouTube channel and for Google Accounts without a linked YouTube account, the yt:username field will not be a traditional YouTube username. Instead, it will be a globally unique identifier that isn't intended for display in a user interface. A new field, yt:userId, will always contain this globally unique identifier regardless of the account type, and if you are writing new code to specifically deal with that identifier, we recommend reading it from yt:userId.

I can't quite figure out where/why you would ever want to use the userId instead of the channelId.  It's possible that users with no uploads don't have a channelId, although that edge-case wouldn't really be applicable to any of our congresspeople.

Although it's apparently [not set in stone](https://developers.google.com/youtube/analytics/v1/channel_reports?hl=en), channelIds typically follow the format of `'UC' + userID`.  According to a YouTube employee on StackOverflow, [this is generally a safe convention](http://stackoverflow.com/a/13105600/334717) to follow if you need to derive one ID from the other.  

In many cases (in the v2 XML API), userIds and channelds can be used interchangeably.  In the v3 REST API, userIds are barely used at all.  I haven't come across any queries that explicitly prefer the userId over the channelId.  Circling back to our original issue, many queries on the v2 API, and all queries on the v3 API don't support using the username, but prefer using one of the two `id` properties.

YouTube seems to be phasing out the concept of "users," in favor of channels.  I haven't been able to find any API requests that prefer using a userId over a channelId (even at that, the two can usually be used interchangeably).

If we're talking about constructing URLs, the following URLs (for Sen. King) are all equivalent:
- http://www.youtube.com/[username]
- http://www.youtube.com/user/[username]
- http://www.youtube.com/channel/[channelId]

In case anybody is somehow still reading this, you can grab a YouTube user's profile (via the v.2.0 XML API) and see how all of this stuff relates in practice by querying:
`http://gdata.youtube.com/feeds/api/users/[userId | channelId | username]?v=2&prettyprint=true`
The v3.0 REST API only supports queries based off of channelId, which is why we probably want to move in that direction...

Committee URLs are handled differently for the House and Senate and I think it's misleading to only link to the majority's site as the official URL for committees in the House. Bear with me as I go into some detail:

The URL structure for the Senate is [committee].senate.gov/public/[party] so it's correct to list the [committee].senate.gov URL for Senate committees because they link out to each party's specific site and the [committee].senate.gov main is not a partisan page (it includes news from both parties). 

In the House it's completely different. The main URL is run by the majority party so [committee].house.gov is partisan. So for this Congress, [committee].house.gov is the Republican site and [Democrats].[committee].house.gov is the minority site. Another thing is that the links between majority and minority sites in the House are often buried in the footer somewhere so it's helpful to have this partisan distinction made at the data level.

The /unitedstates project already has the minority URLs listed in the RSS stuff, so it's just a matter of adding a new `minority_url` field for House committees and dropping in [democrats] before each `url`. Or alternatively having a `url`, `majority_url` and `minority_url` fields so that it's uniform across chambers and each link spells out who runs it.

In whatever language you use, you then can construct the URL from something like:

`"http://bioguide.congress.gov/bioguide/photo/" + bioguide[0] + "/" + bioguide + ".jpg"`

There is not 100% coverage for current members, but it's a good start

Sunlight also offers a set of MoC photos, named by Bioguide ID, for [download as a zip file](http://sunlightlabs.github.io/congress/#legislator-photos). We normalize them into a bunch of different sizes, with the largest being 250x200. 

Even though this project doesn't actually host the MoC photos, the little shell script Sunlight uses to do the resize work [is in it here](https://github.com/unitedstates/congress-legislators/blob/master/scripts/resize-photos.sh), and you could adapt it to your needs. Either way, you'd want to put the result into S3 or something.

The `id` table has a few primary keys (any of them can be used this way), but the best one to use here is `bioguide`. 

The `thomas` ID is to comply with Congress' legacy systems, and the `govtrack` ID is mostly relevant only to GovTrack and sites which may have used its data in the past. Other IDs are provided as we can get them, but don't map as cleanly to the dataset of "members of Congress" as those 3. `bioguide` should always be present.

`other_names` is meant to have any fields that `name` doesn't capture, especially maiden names. It could conceivably contain any field inside `name`, not just `last`. It's basically meant to provide additional names that you'd want to match on searches, rather than being a rigorous way of representing someone's name history.

And yep, `bio` is arbitrary. We just tried to organize these in ways that make rough sense, without creating a heavily nested structure. The most nested is `terms`, which contains the most ephemeral data. If I were doing a more tabular system, I'd split terms out into its own table, for sure.

I just added a note to our README in https://github.com/unitedstates/congress-legislators/commit/718969d5bdeb2020955e065f58a60e058193c4d6 that indicates bioguide is the best primary key. I'm going to close the issue, unless there are other asks.

I've got @lorien working on this problem: using House/Senate votes & Bioguide to determine cases of party changes.

Are we all good with this approach:
- The `party` field is used for the last party affiliation of the person. (That means in current data it is their current party.)
- We add a `party_changes` field inside terms which is a list of dicts containing a party and an end date of all _previous_ party affiliations, if the Member changed party affiliation during the term. The start date could be inferred from the term start (if it's the first record) or the end date of the previous party dict.

There are a few questions that come out of this:
- We could also put a record in `party_changes` for the current party, so that the array has everything.
- We could include start dates too. It would be redundant, but it might help make the data easier to use.
- We might want to figure out if/how we encode how the Member caucuses. An Independent who caucuses with one of the parties changes the majority/minority power structure, but we'd be listing Independent because that's how it would normally appear in the primary source data.

We'll submit a PR if this approach sounds good.

(Also see #10.)

party? To be honest, I don't think having the actual date precisely is that
important so long as it accurately depicts their party affiliation at the
time of a campaign.

needs to be addressed here. But agree that in some cases it's more

> party: The political party of the legislator. If the legislator changed parties, this is the most recent party held during the term and party_affiliations will be set. Values are typically "Democrat", "Independent", or "Republican". The value typically matches the political party of the legislator on the ballot in his or her last election, although for state affiliate parties such as "Democratic Farmer Labor" we will use the national party name ("Democrat") instead to keep the values of this field normalized.
> 
> caucus: For independents, the party that the legislator caucuses with, using the same values as the party field. Omitted if the legislator caucuses with the party indicated in the party field. When in doubt about the difference between the party and caucus fields, the party field is what displays after the legislator's name (i.e. "(D)") but the caucus field is what normally determines committee seniority. This field was added starting with terms for the 113th Congress.
> 
> party_affiliations: This field is present if the legislator changed party or caucus affiliation during the term. The value is a list of time periods, with start and end dates, each of which has a party field and a caucus field if applicable, with the same meanings as the main party and caucus fields. The time periods cover the entire term, so the first start will match the term start, the last end will match the term end, and the last party (and caucus if present) will match the term party (and caucus).

First, I build a database table listing legislators and their data using legislators-current.yaml(or this can be viewed as being specific to a certain congress). Let's call that table 'legislators113', I use the table of that congress's legislators to make an empty table for votes to be added. Column 1 is the bill id, and the rest of the following columns are the legislator ids that can be paired in the vote files. For senators, that is the 'lis' id. 

Then I machine-infer that 2013 or 2014 are part of congress 113 depending which year I am building vote tables for.  A script checks each vote starting with h1 (/113/votes/2013/h1). If the category is not 'passage', or 'passage-suspension', that file is skipped.  It runs through and saves how each legislator voted on each bill in those categories in one big table with about 33k cells for that year.  This can then be repeated for 2014, 2015 etc.

We don't track G+ accounts, and there are only 33 `plus.google.com` URLs in that gist -- plus G+ is a wasteland -- so that doesn't seem worth tracking. We're also not likely to incorporate a Picasa account (e.g.  http://picasaweb.google.com/congresswomanpingree/)

As far as I can tell there are no official records of swearing-in dates for the older sessions. The Senate does have a list of "start of service" dates, but the historian's office says these are not always the same as the date the senator was sworn in. It also appears that for at least some representatives, the start of service listed in Bioguide is the first date of the term's Senate special session (even if the House did not go into session until later).

So it seems like for cases where the swearing-in date is unknown, the choices for default term start dates are:

* Use the first date of the term's first regular session. This is mostly what the data uses now. In years when there was a special session before the first regular session, many/most members' start dates are incorrect, since they would have started at the beginning of the special session. This also leaves out some members' terms entirely (if they served for part/all of a special session but none of the regular session); these cases would have to be fixed manually anyway, but it would lead to lots of inconsistencies in start dates.

* For House terms, use the first date of the House's first special session (if it was before the first regular session). For Senate terms, use the senator's start date (listed here: http://www.senate.gov/artandhistory/history/resources/pdf/chronlist.pdf and in Bioguide).

When it's useful to do this again, here's a quickie script:

```python
import csv,fnmatch,os,re,yaml

with open('congress_fax_data.csv','r') as c:
    cdata = [[w.replace('\xa0','') for w in line] for line in csv.reader(c)]

with open(os.path.expanduser('~/Source/github/essandess/congress-legislators/legislators-current.yaml'),'r') as y:
   ydata = yaml.load(y,Loader=yaml.CLoader)

check = dict()
for line in cdata:
    try:
        cfax = line[-1]
        names = line[0].split(' ')[1:]
        for leg in (leg for leg in ydata if fnmatch.fnmatch(leg['name']['last'],names[-1]) and fnmatch.fnmatch(leg['name']['first'],names[0])):
            yfax = [term['fax'] for term in leg['terms'] if 'fax' in term]
            if cfax not in yfax: check[line[0]] = line[1]
    except:
        pass
for name in check: print('{}: Check fax {}.'.format(name,check[name]))
```

I think I figured out out to cherry-pick the commits to submit a PR with just the lookup script and legislator-current updates. I'm going to close this PR and open a new one with the cherry-picked commits.

For future reference, commit-specific PRs are added with the following process:

1. Create a new master branch with the commits organized as you'd like to submit:

```
cp ./files ~/Downloads
git checkout -b congress-lookup f4c99524c0c2a1d320f4f19babbccadbe5ef2c0c
cp ~/Downloads/file1 .  # use diff to make sure recent updates aren't being copied over
git commit -am 'File 1 comments'
cp ~/Downloads/file2 .  # use diff to make sure recent updates aren't being copied over
git commit -am 'File 2 comments'
git branch -m master old-master
git branch -m congress-lookup master
git push -f origin master
```

2. Cherry-pick these commits within a new `upstream` branch.

```
git remote add upstream https://github.com/unitedstates/congress-legislators.git
git remote update
git checkout -b upstream upstream/master
git cherry-pick 668fe3dfcd25ad1a452a9b8488798e78d4974212
git cherry-pick 479f981ad4a544072cf642f32870189cc7c16879
git push origin upstream
```

3. Use GitHub to issue a PR using the new `upstream` branch, which will have the cherry-picked commits.

I think to faithfully include ICPSR IDs in the current format of the `legislators-*.yaml` files, they would have to be listed with each term and, when applicable, each party affiliation within a term, since members get a new ID if they switch parties or chambers mid-term. So Jim Jeffords, for example, would look like:

```
  - type: sen
    start: '1995-01-04'
    end: '2001-01-03'
    state: VT
    class: 1
    party: Republican
    icpsr: 14240
  - type: sen
    start: '2001-01-03'
    end: '2007-01-03'
    state: VT
    class: 1
    party: Independent
    url: http://jeffords.senate.gov/
    party_affiliations:
    - start: '2001-01-03'
      end: '2001-06-06'
      party: Republican
      icpsr: 14240
    - start: '2001-06-06'
      end: '2007-01-03'
      party: Independent
      icpsr: 94240

I think each user is going to have a different idea of what form of a name they want to display, and keeping first/middle/last separate makes it more flexible.

I don't think having a hard and fast rule about combining first initial and middle name is going to work for all cases; "F. James Sensenbrenner" seems better than "James Sensenbrenner", but "J. Robert Kerrey" seems worse than "Robert Kerrey", and "T. Slade Gorton" worse than "Slade Gorton".

Of the alternatives you mentioned, the third seems best to me, though maybe there are others that would work well.

The way we handled this at Sunlight was to have a separate field: `nickname`, that could be used to reliably display the person's name.

So you might have someone with the fields:

```yaml
first_name: F.
middle_name: James
last_name: Sensenbrenner
nickname: Jim
```

And for someone with no special nickname, the field is just blank or missing:

```yaml
first_name: John
middle_name: Sidney
last_name: McCain
nickname: 
```

This made display logic very easy, at the cost of manually maintaining nickname fields. But the cost of maintaining nickname fields is actually super low -- they're not used by everyone, they basically never change over the course of someone's life (and they're not traditionally affected by marriage like last names can be). So you do them once at election-time, or whenever you eventually notice it, and it flows naturally downstream.

So display logic can be very consistent and simple for those who need it:

* If there's a nickname field, use it
* If not, use the first name field

And I think it gets rid of all the tradeoffs in the approach and alternatives given. Thoughts?

The Congressional Directory was mentioned earlier, but I was looking it over so I thought I'd post more information:

* There is plain-text from GPO going back to 1997: https://www.govinfo.gov/app/collection/cdir
* Some Congresses have more than one update.
* Recent years seem to only have Senate membership (but we have recent years from other sources).
* Some years seem to have subcommittees.

I started writing some code before deciding parsing the plain text would be too hard to get done any time soon, but here's some code to pull down the text files:

	import json
	import urllib.request

	def walk_directory(url):
		print(url + "...")
		directory = json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(url + "?fetchChildrenOnly=1").read().decode("utf8"))
		for node in directory["childNodes"]:
			if node["nodeValue"]["level"] == 3 and node["nodeValue"].get("displayValue", "") != "Committee Assignments":
				# Skip nodes that don't have committee assignments within them.
				pass
			elif "value" in node["nodeValue"]:
				# Recursively go into this node.
				walk_directory(url + "/" + node["nodeValue"]["value"])
			elif re.match("ASSIGNMENTS OF (SENATORS|REPRESENTATIVES) TO COMMITTEES", node["nodeValue"].get("title", "")):
				# This holds committee assignments!
				parse_committee_assignments(node["nodeValue"]["packageid"], node["nodeValue"]["textfile"])

	walk_directory("https://www.govinfo.gov/wssearch/rb/cdir")
